name: Times club monthly special crossword No 286

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Mob from Republican party covering eatery with fliers

indicators.note: a cover goes round whatever it covers, so the outer piece wraps the inner

blocks.note: Sinn Féin, the Irish republican party, abbreviated SF
a caff is a cheap British café
the Royal Air Force, whose members fly

explanation.surface: A mob of party activists surrounds a café, aircraft overhead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Republican' tempts the solver to write R, but the whole phrase is the Irish republican party Sinn Féin, whose two initials go round both other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Scaff-raff is a Scots and dialect form of riff-raff, meaning the rabble or common crowd.

clue.text: Parisian woman of letters disregarding new form of boxing

indicators.note: to disregard something is to leave it out of account, so a letter is dropped

blocks.note: the French feminine of savant, a learned woman
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A French bluestocking takes up a novel style of boxing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parisian' signals a French word: a female scholar is une savante; take out its N.
explanation.definitionFit: Savate is French kickboxing, a combat sport in which both feet and fists are used.

clue.text: Promoting commercial it’s not a reason for swallowing pain

blocks.note: read with 'not': not promoting an advert means being against it, ANTI plus AD
the contraction written out in full

explanation.surface: Someone declares they are not promoting a commercial as a reason for something.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange the opening as 'it's not promoting commercial': that person is anti-ad, it is. The -ITIS ending then completes a medical word.
explanation.definitionFit: Antiaditis is an old term for tonsillitis, inflammation of the tonsils, which makes swallowing painful.

clue.text: Maltese cape where third parts of fertile alluvial area change over

indicators.note: points at the letter in third position of each of two words
changing over means swapping places, so those two letters trade positions

blocks.note: fat land is rich and productive
a river delta is built of alluvial deposits

explanation.surface: A cape from Malta is described in terms of farmland and river silt.
explanation.walkthrough: FAT and DELTA swap their third letters, T and L, giving FAL and DETTA.
explanation.definitionFit: The faldetta is a traditional Maltese woman's garment, a hooded cape or mantle worn over the head and shoulders.

clue.text: Classical pianist pairs read up on loss of odd parts

indicators.note: losing the odd-numbered letters leaves only the even ones

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on

explanation.surface: A concert pianist reads up on duets before a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pairs' looks like part of the musician's story but is fodder; strip letters 1, 3, 5 and onward from the three words run together.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudio Arrau was a celebrated Chilean concert pianist known for Beethoven and Liszt.

clue.text: Thanks to Japan surrendering lead for fine working ship in Venice

indicators.note: giving up the leading letter in exchange for another one replaces the first letter

blocks.note: arigato is Japanese for thank you
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
a machine that is working is on

explanation.surface: A Venetian ship is crewed, it seems, by grateful Japanese sailors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thanks to Japan' reads like gratitude to a country, but it is Japanese for thanks; its A becomes F.
explanation.definitionFit: A frigatoon is a square-sterned Venetian sailing vessel of the Adriatic, so it is literally a ship from that city.

clue.text: Dandy spurning one of each side makes a leisurely journey

indicators.note: to spurn is to reject, so letters are thrown out

blocks.note: Beau Brummell, the Regency dandy
right and left, one R and one L

explanation.surface: A fop avoids taking sides and goes off on a gentle trip.
explanation.walkthrough: Beau Brummell was the Regency man of fashion; take out one R and one L, the two sides being right and left.
explanation.definitionFit: Bummel is a German borrowing for a stroll or unhurried trip, a ramble without pressing purpose.

clue.text: Steep decline of Henry with fist mostly raised for boxing

indicators.note: most but not all of the word is kept, so its final letter goes
in a down clue, lifting a word up makes it read from bottom to top
a box holds its contents, so this piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
dukes is slang for fists

explanation.surface: A boxer called Henry is on the slide, fist up for the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxing' belongs to the fist-fighting picture but here means enclosing. Dukes, as in 'put up your dukes', is slang for fists.
explanation.definitionFit: Khud is an Anglo-Indian word for a precipice or steep hillside, a ravine dropping sharply away.

clue.text: Training day includes time in Kiwi country to get rock used in China

indicators.note: to include something is to hold it within, so one part sits inside another
one thing sitting in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: physical education, school exercise training
the abbreviation for Tuesday
T is the abbreviation for time
New Zealand, home of the Kiwis

explanation.surface: Someone on a training day in New Zealand comes away with a rock used in Chinese porcelain.
explanation.walkthrough: Two nested containers: T goes inside NZ, and that pair goes inside the abbreviated weekday. 'China' with a capital is the country, though the rock does end up in china.
explanation.definitionFit: Petuntze is a feldspathic stone ground and mixed with kaolin to make Chinese porcelain.

clue.text: Scot’s generous welcome during regular journey

indicators.note: something happening during another thing occurs within it, so one piece sits inside

blocks.note: a greeting
a route is the course regularly travelled, as by a bus

explanation.surface: A Scotsman greets people warmly along his usual way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scot's' marks a Scots dialect word, and 'welcome' is the greeting rather than the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Routhie is Scots for plentiful or abundant, so it describes something given in generous measure.

clue.text: Agriculturalist almost breaks through resistance of calves

indicators.note: almost all means one letter short, so the last is dropped
breaking into something means getting inside it

blocks.note: Jethro Tull, the English agricultural pioneer who invented the seed drill
by way of
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A farmer nearly breaks through the resistance of his young cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: The agriculturalist is Jethro Tull, the eighteenth-century farming innovator, not the rock band named after him. 'Of calves' looks like part of the resistance but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Vitular is an adjective from Latin vitulus, a calf, meaning relating to calves.

clue.text: Spinning, stretch in quad-emphasising form of exercise

indicators.note: a stretch is a continuous run of something, here a run of letters inside the words
something spinning turns round, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: the run of letters straddling the hyphen

explanation.surface: A gym routine of spinning and stretching that works the thigh muscles.
explanation.walkthrough: Spinning and stretching sound like gym activities; in fact they signal turning letters round and taking a run of them. Quad is gym slang for the quadriceps.
explanation.definitionFit: Medau is a system of rhythmic movement and breathing exercises devised by Hinrich Medau, used in keep-fit classes.

clue.text: Supporting band’s meaningless lyric including “live, see you in DMs”

indicators.note: to include is to take within, so the outer word holds the others

blocks.note: tra-la, a nonsense refrain in songs
to live is to exist, to be
text-speak in direct messages for 'see you'

explanation.surface: A support act's nonsense song invites fans to chat by direct message.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supporting band' suggests a group opening a gig, but it is an anatomical strand. DMs are direct messages on social media, where CU is shorthand.
explanation.definitionFit: A trabecula is a small bar, strand or septum of tissue that supports or divides an organ or bone.

clue.text: Palm and ankle bones fitting exactly

blocks.note: plural of talus, the anklebone
as in 'off pat' or 'just pat', exactly suitable

explanation.surface: Hand and foot bones slot together neatly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palm' sits beside ankle bones to suggest the hand, but it is the tree. Pat as an adjective means apt or exactly right.
explanation.definitionFit: The talipat, or talipot, is a tall fan palm of southern India and Sri Lanka.

clue.text: Australian herb in pop with aniseed-flavoured spirit lay in ferment

indicators.note: fermenting liquid is agitated and churned, so the letters are stirred up

blocks.note: pop and pa are both words for father
a variant spelling of raki, the anise liqueur of Turkey and the Balkans
taken as written

explanation.surface: Fizzy drink mixed with an aniseed spirit lies fermenting, with a herb added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pop' suggests fizzy drink but is father. The spirit must be the less familiar spelling rakee to fit.
explanation.definitionFit: Parakeelya is an Australian succulent plant of the purslane family, eaten by stock in arid country.

clue.text: Neglect to pen book about climber in Amazon

indicators.note: to pen is to shut in an enclosure, so one piece goes inside the other
about can mean turned round, so the result reads backwards

blocks.note: to omit is to neglect or leave out
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: Someone fails to write a book on climbing in the Amazon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Climber' suggests a mountaineer, but it is a climbing plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Timbo is a South American woody vine whose roots yield a fish poison and insecticide, so it is a plant climber.

clue.text: Long-lived French president curbing unending prejudice

indicators.note: with no end, the final letter is taken off
to curb is to restrain or hold in, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: Emmanuel Macron
bias is prejudice

explanation.surface: A durable French head of state restrains endless bias.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Long-lived' reads as a description of the president but stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Macrobian means living a long time, from Greek makros, long, and bios, life.

clue.text: Missing son, off course after cycling pilgrimage in India

indicators.note: if something is missing it is absent, so a letter is dropped
going round in a cycle moves a letter from one end of the word to the other

blocks.note: S is the genealogical abbreviation for son
astray means away from the right course

explanation.surface: A son goes missing, having wandered off on a cycling tour of India.
explanation.walkthrough: Without S the adverb becomes ATRAY; cycling then brings its final Y round to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Yatra is the Hindi and Sanskrit word for a journey, especially a religious pilgrimage to a holy site.

clue.text: Digger’s horse upset SE Asian war arrangement

indicators.note: in a down clue, upsetting turns things upside down, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: short for Vietnam, the war
an array is an orderly arrangement

explanation.surface: An Australian soldier's horse is spooked by the arrangements for war in South-East Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: Digger is slang for an Australian soldier, so the word is Australian. Nam was the soldiers' name for the Vietnam War, in which Australians fought.
explanation.definitionFit: Yarraman is an Australian word, probably from an Aboriginal language, for a horse.

clue.text: Pierre’s body temperature not so good when losing weight

indicators.note: losing something means parting with it, so a letter goes

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for temperature
the comparative of bad
W is the abbreviation for weight

explanation.surface: A Frenchman's body temperature worsens as he loses weight.
explanation.walkthrough: Pierre stands for any Frenchman, so the definition asks for a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: Torse is the French for the trunk or torso of the human figure.

clue.text: University requirement repeatedly dropping mark over wrapping art

indicators.note: dropping something lets it fall away, so a letter is lost
turned over, the whole string is flipped to read the other way

blocks.note: U is the abbreviation for university
a must is a requirement, and 'repeatedly' doubles it
M for mark, the old German currency

explanation.surface: A university keeps insisting on a skill, docking marks for wrapping presents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' sounds like a grade, but it is the abbreviation M, removed from the second of the two requirements. In a down clue the whole string is then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Tsutsumu is the Japanese art of wrapping gifts and objects decoratively, the verb meaning to wrap.

clue.text: Part of your heart’s constant burden

blocks.note: C is the symbol for a constant, as in the speed of light
an onus is a burden or responsibility

explanation.surface: A lover complains that their heart carries a constant burden.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as possessive but stands for 'is', linking definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The conus arteriosus is the cone-shaped upper part of the right ventricle, leading to the pulmonary artery.

clue.text: Perhaps making more noise with paper, having dismissed inventory’s head stocktaker

indicators.note: the head of something is its top or front, so only the opening letter is wanted
dismissing someone sends them away, so a letter leaves

blocks.note: the comparative of rustly, making a crackling sound
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone noisily rustles papers while doing an inventory and stocktake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stocktaker' looks like an auditor counting the inventory; read literally it is someone who takes livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: A rustler steals cattle or horses, so in a cryptic sense he literally takes stock.

clue.text: Previous descent from small horse covered by very basic solution

indicators.note: whatever is covered lies under and inside its covering

blocks.note: lye is a strongly alkaline solution, basic in the chemical sense
a nag is a small or worn-out horse

explanation.surface: A pony's ancestry is buried under a very simple answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basic' looks like simple, but it is the chemistry sense, alkaline. 'Previous' signals an obsolete spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Lynage is an old spelling of lineage, line of ancestry, so it is an earlier form of the word.

clue.text: Morally repudiating church’s lack of a central core

indicators.note: repudiating something is disowning it, so those letters are cast off

blocks.note: in a chaste, virtuous manner
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Moral objections to a church lacking a heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove CH from the adverb. The definition is a botanical noun, which makes 'central core' read as a plant stem's structure rather than a church's spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Astely in botany is the absence of a stele, the vascular cylinder running through the middle of stems and roots.

clue.text: Being morally required, thug crashed into a person’s Sierra

indicators.note: a crash smashes things into a jumble
putting one thing into another places it inside

blocks.note: taken as written
one's, the impersonal possessive
Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A thug, feeling obliged, crashes a stolen Ford Sierra belonging to someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Sierra looks like a car model (a Ford Sierra was a common British family car) but is the phonetic-alphabet letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Oughtness is the quality of being obligatory, the state of being something one ought to do.

clue.text: Fish relish sport among group of whales

indicators.note: whatever sits among others is surrounded on every side by them

blocks.note: a gam is a school of whales
rugby union

explanation.surface: Fish enjoy playing games among a pod of whales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' looks like a verb of enjoyment but is a noun, a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Garum was the fermented fish sauce of ancient Rome, used as a condiment or relish.

clue.text: Chinese official’s American denunciation

blocks.note: AM is the abbreviation for American
a ban in the old sense of a curse or public condemnation

explanation.surface: A Chinese official is denounced by the Americans.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s stands for 'is'. Ban here keeps its old meaning of curse or anathema.
explanation.definitionFit: An amban was a Manchu imperial resident or high official posted to Tibet or Mongolia under the Qing.

clue.text: Large transport centre sent up inlaid furniture

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending something upwards makes it read bottom to top

blocks.note: L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
a hub is a central point of a transport network

explanation.surface: A big transport depot ships its inlaid furniture upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' could mean mocked; in this down clue it turns the letters to read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Buhl is furniture decorated with marquetry of brass and tortoiseshell, named after the cabinetmaker Boulle.

clue.text: Without question, French article on cooking stock recalled Provençal sauce

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is left out
calling something back makes it go back the way it came
in an across clue, one thing placed on another follows it, so the preceding piece is written second

blocks.note: in cookery, liquor is the liquid or stock that food has cooked in
Q is the abbreviation for question
the masculine definite article in French

explanation.surface: A French cook confidently explains that a Provençal sauce is made from recalled stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without question' reads as 'certainly', but it means remove Q. With 'on' in an across clue the article comes after the other piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Rouille is a garlicky, rust-coloured sauce of chilli and bread or potato, served with bouillabaisse in Provence.

clue.text: Refusal to swallow Samoan port plugged by enchanting woman

indicators.note: a plug fills a hole, so one piece is pushed into the other

blocks.note: Apia is the capital and main port of Samoa
a hag in the sense of a witch, one who casts spells

explanation.surface: A charming woman refuses to swallow the story of a Samoan port.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Enchanting' suggests charming, but here it means casting spells, which makes the woman a witch.
explanation.definitionFit: Aphagia is the medical term for an inability or refusal to swallow, from Greek for 'not eating'.

clue.text: Largely insensitive rejection of younger ex-student in States of Change?

indicators.note: largely means for the most part, so the word loses its last letter
something rejected is sent back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: numb means without feeling
YR is the abbreviation for younger
alum, short for alumnus, is the American term for a former student

explanation.surface: A heartless snub of a younger graduate in the changing American states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In States' tells you the ex-student word is American usage. The capital C on 'Change' disguises plain coins, and the question mark flags the pun.
explanation.definitionFit: Nummulary means relating to coins or money, and change is a word for loose coins.
